places.short: At 2,826 m, the only road into Tusheti: some 70 km of narrow gravel from Pshaveli to Omalo, open roughly June to mid-October, 4x4 only.
Brick domes breathing sulphur at the foot of Narikala: the warm springs that gave Tbilisi its name, still filling private stone pools by the hour.
A 30-metre fall at the very source of the Abasha, in dense box forest five kilometres from Second Balda, reached only by a slow, hard forest track.
White domes in the pines of Mount Kanobili, where Georgian astronomy began in 1932, above the faded imperial spa of Abastumani.
An old imperial-era spa in a pine valley at 1,340 m: hot springs, a grand duke's legacy and a copy of Zarzma painted by Mikhail Nesterov.
Three glacial lakes under Chaukhi, green, blue and a milky white one at the glacier's foot above 2,800 m, seven kilometres on foot or horseback from Roshka.
A Bronze Age fortress of mortarless basalt at 2,670 m on Mount Patara Abuli, above Lake Paravani: never excavated, still unexplained.
A small hall church south of Ozurgeti with late-13th-century Palaeologan frescoes, a rare cycle of St George and the Greek name of a painter from Trebizond.
The source of the Adishchala: a 9.5 km glacier under Tetnuldi, slowly retreating, an hour or two's walk up the valley from Adishi.
A Svan village at 2,040 m with towers, four medieval churches and a bridgeless glacial river — for centuries the keeper of a Gospel book of 897.
Pirosmani, Kakabadze and Gudiashvili in a white Stalin-era palace on Gorgiladze Street, which until 1998 was a museum of the revolution.
A German colonists' village road turned grand avenue on the left bank: restored facades, iron balconies and a car-free stretch that wakes at dusk.
A great lowland oak wood between Baghdati and Zestaponi, protected since 1935 and a refuge for the relict Imeretian oak and zelkova.
The convent a queen built after leaving her king: a 16th-century brick church, and on her tombstone the oldest surviving Bagrationi coat of arms.
An 11th-century citadel on the spur between two canyons, in the Javakheti plateau's main town: 1,700 metres up, Armenian-speaking and wind-scoured.

places.n: The Jewish quarter and synagogues of Akhaltsikhe
places.short: A synagogue of 1862 with a painted wooden interior, its empty younger neighbour and an old hillside cemetery in Akhaltsikhe's Rabati district.
Warm grey mud wells up in the middle of Gurjaani: a mud-cure resort since 1920, and every October the grounds of Georgia's biggest wine festival.
Kvirike III's 11th-century cathedral, over fifty metres tall and alone on the Alazani plain — for nearly a thousand years Georgia's tallest church.
A long green trough of vineyards between Gombori and the Caucasus: Strabo's Alazonius, medieval Hereti, and the heart of Georgian wine.
Georgia's easternmost spruce and fir, protected since 1965 on the Trialeti slopes above Manglisi: cool forest, five trails and very few people.
Tamara Kvesitadze's eight-metre steel lovers on Batumi's waterfront: each evening they glide together, pass through each other and part.
A small gallery in Racha's capital holding 565 works by 20th-century Georgian artists, from Lado Gudiashvili to Elene Akhvlediani and David Kakabadze.
Georgia's smallest regional capital, astride the Rioni at 550 metres: a princely tower, a fine-arts museum, Racha's table and your last easy fuel.
Three 17th–18th-century castles of the Amilakhvari princes at Kvemo Chala: towers, a church with fresco fragments, an unfinished belfry and a domed bathhouse.
A half-built resort, a 540-metre footbridge and empty sand where the Enguri meets the sea — and a history far older than the concrete.
Two castles, two churches and a tower with a terrible past above the Zhinvali reservoir — the first great stop on the road to Kazbegi.
Slate burial vaults on a bluff above the Arghuni near Shatili: bones behind iron grilles, a plague legend everyone tells, and a quieter truth scholars suggest.
Tbilisi's oldest surviving church: a sixth-century basilica on Shavteli Street, low and dim, where Georgian polyphony still fills the stone.
A towered fortress-hall on the Prone river, wrapped around the church Queen Mariam built in 1666, a short hop off the motorway at Kareli.
A 1959 obelisk above the Mtkvari at Ortachala, raised where remains of Tbilisi's defenders of 1795 were unearthed.
A Khevsur border valley beyond the end of the road, reached only by jeep track or on foot, where two villages still keep their hearths burning.
The hilltop citadel of pagan Iberia, facing Mtskheta across the Mtkvari: palace footings, a Roman-age bath house and, most days, nobody else.
A Gothic-Moorish palace built for a scandalous love affair, now home to 300,000 objects from Georgian theatre, film, opera and dance.
A small limestone canyon above Dedoplistskaro where griffon vultures and black storks nest, and a bellflower grows that exists nowhere else.
Small glaciers and the Assa's last Georgian gorge before Ingushetia: no road, no ticket office, only a long guided walk in.
A broken tower above the Bakhvistsqali at Mtispiri: once Guria's treasury and prison, besieged until 1828, now swallowed by forest.
The Swabian colony of Elisabethtal, founded in 1818: tiled gables, deep wine cellars, a Lutheran church of 1871 and a grape first found in the woods.
A 7th-century church on a cliff above the Tana, where the script on every Georgian shop sign first appears in a dated inscription.
Family cellars in the Tana gorge south of Gori, home of Atenuri: a crisp, pale sparkling white made from Chinuri and Goruli Mtsvane.
A fortress on a sheer cliff where the Mtkvari gorge narrows between Borjomi and Akhaltsikhe, above the ruins of a cathedral that once held a famous icon.
The forester’s house in Baghdati where Vladimir Mayakovsky, the loudest poet of the Russian avant-garde, was born and learned Georgian.
Bagrat III's cathedral of 1003 on Ukimerioni Hill, blown up by an Ottoman garrison and controversially rebuilt, above the old heart of Kutaisi.
A summer-only resort of stilted timber cottages at about 1,950 m in the Guria mountains, where a sea breeze climbs the valley to meet the spruce.
Seventeen hectares at 1,700 metres on the edge of Bakuriani, where scientists have been coaxing plants of the high Caucasus into bloom since 1910.
Georgia's oldest winter resort, 1,700 metres up in a spruce-dark volcanic basin above Borjomi: gentle pistes in winter, cool air all summer.
A 1.4 km limestone slot cut by the Abasha river beside Balda monastery: narrow, green-walled and far quieter than Martvili Canyon.

places.n: Bank of Georgia Headquarters (former Ministry of Highways)
places.short: A 1975 Brutalist landmark of five two-storey concrete blocks stacked crosswise over a wooded slope — built for Soviet road-builders, now a bank.
Built in 1753 for Duke Rostom of Racha on a cliff where the Lukhuni meets the Rioni — one of the last great domed churches of old Georgia.
A shallow, rain-fed natural lake at 1,612 m on the open Trialeti plateau, full of waterfowl in season — the wild neighbour of the Tsalka Reservoir.
The gateway village of Khevsureti on the Aragvi: guesthouses, a hot meal and a long memory before the road turns into a 4x4 track.
A tiny landslide lake in the forests of the Dzama valley at 1,313 m; in late October the beeches burn crimson and double themselves in the water.
A side gorge of Pankisi shelters the largest yew forest on earth, where a few trees are thought to be some 1,500 years old.
An old lakeside park in central Batumi and a dolphinarium whose 1974 mosaic dolphins still swim across its outer wall.
A 130-metre double helix carrying the 33 glowing letters of the Georgian alphabet, with Ali and Nino coming to life at its foot at 7 pm.
Greek and Colchian graves from Pichvnari, coins from Gonio and a room of gold: Adjara's deep past on two floors of a grey stone building.
Two and a half kilometres of air from Batumi's port to Anuria hill, where the whole city lies spread out like a map by the sea.
Nine floristic worlds on Green Cape above the sea, in the garden where Georgia's tea, citrus and eucalyptus began.
A seafront promenade planted on bare sand in 1881, and an old town built on oil money, with iron balconies and a Gothic Revival cathedral.

places.n: Batumi Cathedral of the Mother of God
places.short: A Gothic Revival church of pale stone, built for Georgian Catholics in 1898–1903, a physics laboratory in Soviet years, now Batumi's Orthodox cathedral.
Where Batumi's Old and New Boulevards meet, Ardagani Lake becomes a stage on summer nights: French-built fountains, music and lasers on a curtain of spray.
On Baku Street by the port you pick your Black Sea fish off the ice and carry it next door to be fried: a Batumi meal that starts at the counter.
Batumi's only working mosque, built in 1866 for a Muslim Georgian noble family: a golden dome, walls painted by Laz masters, Friday prayers in the street.
An Italianate square in Old Batumi, built in 2009, whose floor is a 106 m² marble mosaic of five sea goddesses laid in just ten days.
Batumi's 1904 Ashkenazi synagogue became a Soviet sports hall in 1923 and was returned only in 1998; today it is a house of prayer again, near the boulevard.
A small, warm lake south of Dusheti, where folklore keeps a golden cradle on the bottom and Ilia Chavchavadze set it to verse in 1883.
An ancient fortress on a spur above the Aragvi at Mtskheta's northern gate, where King Demetre I died in 1156 — free, unfenced and open to the sky.
The Dolra valley below Ushba's twin summits: Mazeri at 1,660 m, a 120-metre waterfall fed by the Ushba glacier, and the quiet Mestia has lost.
A monastery on the western shore of Tsalka Reservoir whose main church stands over a karst spring — with trout living in the pool beneath the floor.
A Pontic Greek village on the Trialeti plateau, named after 'Five Stones' in Anatolia, beside a Bronze Age cyclopean settlement and cemetery.
A summer village of wooden, tin-roofed cottages near the Goderdzi Pass, alive from June to September and snowbound the rest of the year.
A Golden Age monastery deep in the wooded Vere gorge, where Queen Tamar looks out from a fresco painted in her own lifetime.
A street that turns into a stone stair below Narikala: two Bethlehem churches, a Sasanian-era fire temple and washing lines over old Tbilisi.
A maze of volcanic rock needles in the Algeti valley, walled into a fortress that Timur could take only by rope ladder at night.
A glacial lake on the Georgia–Dagestan crest at about 2,800 m, reached only on foot: a 38 km loop through Georgia's oldest nature reserve.
A church of the 1180s, named for its long-lost blue-glazed roof tiles, standing quietly among the houses of Vera a few minutes from Rustaveli.
St Nino's resting place above the Alazani Valley: a low basilica among cypresses, a working convent, and a steep path down to her spring.
Georgia's oldest standing church, finished in 493–494 near Bolnisi, still carries the dated Georgian inscriptions its builders cut into the stone.
Katharinenfeld, the Swabian colony of 1818: straight streets of German houses, Mill Street, a museum opened in 2020, and vineyards and copper all around.

places.n: Borjomi Central Park and Mineral Springs
places.short: A 19th-century spa park in a narrow wooded gorge, where you fill your own bottle with salty, faintly warm Borjomi water straight from the spring.
More than one per cent of Georgia under forest and meadow, crossed by marked trails with mountain shelters, beginning at the edge of Borjomi.
The Romanov estate's old chancellery, a pseudo-Gothic house that now keeps palace tableware, the mineral-water story and the valley's wildlife.

places.n: Bridge of Peace and Rike Park
places.short: A glass-and-steel wave over the Mtkvari that lights up under your footsteps, and the riverside park where the cable car sets off for Narikala.
Batumi's 1975 'Octopus': a mosaic-clad iron gridshell on the seafront, abandoned in 2000, defended by the city and listed as a monument in 2020.
Clay badlands and Iori riverine forest on the Azerbaijani border, where griffon and Egyptian vultures breed and imperial eagles hunt.
The lowest-reaching glacier on the Caucasus's southern flank: grey ice pushing into the forest, an hour's walk from a trailhead 8 km above Mestia.
The 19th-century palace and winery of Prince Ivane Mukhranbatoni, whose European-style wine won gold in Paris in 1889, working again on the Mukhrani plain.
A manganese town at the bottom of the Kvirila gorge, where cable cars have lifted miners up the cliffs since 1954 and still carry the daily commute.
The last village before Ghebi on the upper Rioni: 116 people, stone houses, and a name that legend traces to the foxes and martens of a riverside meadow.
A small Gurian town where the plain meets the mountains: the last fuel before Bakhmaro, and a past of garrisons, revolts and tea.
Sixteen pillars up to 35 metres high on Keeni Hill above the Tbilisi Sea: Zurab Tsereteli's unfinished epic of bronze and stone.
The palaces of the princes of Mingrelia in a garden first planted in 1840, with a bronze death mask of Napoleon and the robe venerated as the Virgin's.
An 11th–12th-century limestone bridge that bends across the Adjaristsqali in an S, 60 km upriver from Batumi, still with no parapet.

places.n: Dariali Gorge and the Gveleti Waterfalls
places.short: The 'Gate of the Alans': the Tergi's kilometre-deep granite gorge at the Russian border, with the 30-metre Gveleti falls and a monastery consecrated in 2011.
A Tusheti stone village at 2,000 m, with slate roofs, medieval towers and sun signs carved into its walls. Busy in summer, empty all winter.
An eight-kilometre basalt gorge near Tsalka where springs burst from the rock as waterfalls, while the glass Diamond Bridge hangs overhead.
The 2,680-metre gravel pass on the Caucasus watershed that splits Khevsureti in two: the only road to Shatili, open only in the warm months.
A bare ridge on the Azerbaijani border where monks have lived in rock-cut cells since the 6th century, amid semi-desert steppe.
The riverside park where Georgians defended their language in 1978: a bronze monument, a skatepark and the Dry Bridge flea market next door.
The frontier town of the Shiraki plain: David the Builder's outpost, a Russian fort, a Siemens oil venture and the gateway to Vashlovani.
Tbilisi's biggest farmers' market, beside the central station: rows of cheese, heaps of spices, strings of churchkhela and a city bargaining out loud.
Giant swords stand in the turf at 1,650 metres where, on 12 August 1121, David the Builder broke a far larger Seljuk-led coalition.
The extinct 3,301 m volcano west of Lake Paravani: two hours on foot from the end of a 4x4 track to a summit above a plateau scattered with lakes.
A ruined medieval silk town above the Mashavera, and beneath its cellars 1.8-million-year-old skulls from one of humanity's earliest journeys out of Africa.
A stone bridge left high and dry in the 1930s, now spread with Soviet medals, cameras, enamel, samovars and the leftovers of family life.
The largest village of the Pankisi Gorge and heart of Georgia's Kist community, with an early-20th-century mosque and its brick-patterned minaret.
Old seat of the dukes of Aragvi, where Giorgi Saakadze once hid from assassins: today a khinkali and fuel stop on the road to the mountains.
The excavated remains of Zalissa, a town Ptolemy listed among Iberia's chief cities: palaces, Roman-style baths and one of the Caucasus's oldest mosaics.
Three stone churches of the 5th and 7th centuries in the Gombori forest above Telavi — the monks long gone, the clearing left to trees and quiet.
The world's second-highest concrete arch dam: 271.5 metres of curved concrete on the road to Svaneti, holding back a long lake of glacier water.
A 13th-century church south of Kaspi with a carved cross on every façade, 1654 frescoes of its martyr saint and the Saakadze family tombs.
Batumi's grand square: Medea on her column with the Golden Fleece, restored facades and a German astronomical clock.
A Soviet sewing factory turned into a courtyard of bars, studios and a hostel, set in Chughureti — an old left-bank district not yet polished into a set.

places.n: Freedom Square and the Old Parliament
places.short: Tbilisi's central square has changed its name with every new master, from a Russian general to Beria and Lenin; today St George rides above the traffic.
A leaning clock tower on Shavteli Street where an angel steps out every hour, and beside it Rezo Gabriadze's eighty-seat marionette theatre.
Flood-fed poplar and willow jungle on the Mtkvari by the Azerbaijani border: 135 bird species, red deer and no infrastructure whatsoever.
Brick ruins of George III's great palace on the Rioni plain south of Kutaisi, where in 1191 rebel nobles crowned a rival to Queen Tamar.
David the Builder's monastery and academy above Kutaisi: a gold 12th-century mosaic, a royal burial ground, and the king himself under the gate.
The Janashia Museum on Rustaveli Avenue: 1.8-million-year-old Dmanisi skulls, Colchian gold and a sober hall on the Soviet occupation.
A 14th-century church alone on a green crest at 2,170 m under Mount Kazbek: the chief shrine of Khevi, once the hiding place of St Nino's Cross.
A stone village high on the Rioni, recorded since 1503, where a legend of revolt against the lords is still honoured with funeral bread.
Below Lower Ghvirishi a stream leaps from a high rock into a narrow ravine: the loudest, easiest stop on a Tsageri day loop.
A village on the Chanchakhi, 5 km below Shovi, with glacier-borne boulders as big as houses and a ruined citadel on a rocky crag.

places.n: Goderdzi Pass and the Petrified Forest
places.short: A 2,025-metre saddle between sea-damp Adjara and dry Samtskhe, where a forest of palms and laurels lies turned to stone on the eastern slope.
A square stone tower on the ridge above Borjomi, a 10–20-minute climb from the centre, with the whole spa valley laid out at your feet.
Timber oda houses up to 250 years old above the Shareula, their balconies cut with crosses, birds and animals, and still waiting for rescue.
A 1,620-metre crossing on the Sh38 where Outer Kakheti ends and the road tips down towards the Alazani valley and the wall of the Caucasus.
A summer town of timber cottages at about 2,100 m on the Meskheti Range, where dawn often finds the Guria lowland drowned in cloud below.
A Roman fort at the mouth of the Chorokhi: walls of dressed blocks, Ottoman patching, and two graves no one can prove.
A citadel on a rock above the Mtkvari and the Liakhvi, and below it the shrine Gori built to its most notorious son: one town, two views of history.

places.n: Gori War Museum and War Memorial
places.short: A small Museum of Military Glory on Stalin Avenue and Giorgi Ochiauri's ring of bronze warriors below the fortress: Gori's quieter reckoning with war.
A rebuilt church of St George on the hill above Gori, ringed by a broken ancient wall, with Gori's best-known view over the town and the Mtkvari.
A mound beside the Tbilisi–Gori motorway, found by road-builders in 2007, where a goddess's temple hid signs that may be the Caucasus's oldest script.
Mtsvane Tba, the Green Lake: five hectares of cold, clear water at 2,058 m near Goderdzi Pass, and more than nineteen metres deep.
A 9th–10th-century basilica of green-tinged stone in a wooded gorge near Borjomi, abandoned for two centuries and alive again since 2003.
A brick church, a royal tower and a painted king holding his own church, on the hill of Kakheti's lost capital above the Intsoba river.
A quiet shore village of dark magnetic sand and pines, with the Kolkheti wetlands pressing right up behind the beach.
A 13th-century monastery on a wooded hill above Tetritskaro, with the oldest dated bell tower in Georgia, finished in 1278.
Georgia's best-known ski resort, on treeless slopes below the Jvari Pass: lifts to 3,279 metres, six months of snow and summer paragliders.
Georgia's only surviving two-domed church: an 8th–9th-century basilica of river cobble and brick in the quiet Kakhtubani valley outside Gurjaani.
Mestia's two ski areas: Hatsvali, a cable-car ride from town, and Tetnuldi, whose 9.5 km run is the longest in the South Caucasus.
Georgia's main cathedral, consecrated on Elia Hill in 2004: a golden cross 86 metres above the ground, nine chapels, and a city that still argues about it.
Saint Zenon's 6th-century monastery west of Telavi, and the roofless hall of the medieval academy where, tradition says, Rustaveli studied.
Ilia Chavchavadze's birthplace in Kvareli: a 17th-century tower, a 500-year-old walnut, a cellar of 37 qvevri and a mill still turning on the Duruji.
A small wooded lake on Kvareli's western edge, with the Caucasus as its backdrop: Kakheti's summer swim, two kilometres from Ilia Chavchavadze's birthplace.
A plain stone box in Upper Svaneti holding frescoes dated 1096: the first of the three Svan churches painted by the master Tevdore.
Volcanic lakes near 2,000 m on the treeless Javakheti plateau, a haunt of pelicans, storks and ducks that carries on across the border into Armenia.
A wild two-storey karst cave above the Jortsku stream near Martvili, reached on foot, where cave-bear bones lay buried in the clay.
Old Tbilisi's last surviving mosque, at the foot of Narikala: red brick, an octagonal minaret, two mihrabs, and Sunnis and Shias praying in one hall.
A hilltop monastery of the Archangels above the Supsa valley. Its Byzantine enamels are in New York and St Petersburg; its horizon is still here.
A Khevi village at 2,200 m, settled by Khevsurs in the 18th century, under the pale towers of Chaukhi rising to 3,842 m.
A church of about 600 on a cliff above the meeting of the Aragvi and Mtkvari, with carved princes on its walls and Mtskheta spread out below.

places.n: Jvari Pass and the Friendship Monument
places.short: A 1983 concrete arc lined with tiled history above the Devil's Valley, just below Jvari Pass, the Military Highway's high point at 2,379 metres.
Twenty metres of aluminium on the Sololaki ridge: a bowl of wine for friends, a sword for enemies, and the whole Old Town at her feet.
The stone church facing Parliament on Rustaveli: a legend in its name, Samtavisi in its lines, and paintings that cost Lado Gudiashvili his post.
A working parish church in the centre of Kaspi, one of Georgia's oldest towns and once the seat of a 5th-century military governor.
A 40-metre limestone column above the Katskhuri valley, crowned by a restored medieval hermitage; since 2012 visitors admire it from below.

places.n: Keda and the Adjaran Wine Cellars
places.short: A river town on the old road inland from Batumi, where Chkhaveri, one of Georgia's latest-ripening grapes, is picked after mid-November.
A side valley above Kvesheti that an old verse credits with sixty towers, and a thousand-year-old church carved with the men who built it.
A railway town in the deep Chkherimela gorge and the western doorstep of Borjomi-Kharagauli National Park — the beech forest begins where the platform ends.
A 7.7-kilometre network of tunnels cut into the Caucasus rock at Kvareli, opened in 1962, where wine ages at a steady 12–16°C.
A railway town on the western rim of Shida Kartli, where the main road splits: south to Borjomi, west over the Rikoti pass to the sea.
A fortress on a rock spur where the Paravani flows into the Mtkvari, its tower and walls dated by inscription to 1354–1356. On the road to Vardzia.
A ruined stronghold above 2,000 metres at the head of the Skhalta valley, where the rebel pasha Selim Khimshiashvili made his last stand in 1815.
A domed church of sandstone and brick at Tibaani, where a stone dated 886 sits upside down in an arch beneath the dome.
The Dadiani family abbey near Khobi: a carved 13th-century church with an open gallery, princely portraits and Byzantine marble won in a medieval war.
Ruined walls on a lone pale-grey crag above Dedoplistskaro, where a 5th-century king seated a bishop and the plain gives way to steppe.

places.n: Khulo Cable Car and Upper Adjara
places.short: Khulo, old caravan town of Upper Adjara, and the silent Tago cable car: one 1,720-metre span over the gorge, closed since 2024.
A 35–40 km ribbon of south-facing vineyards on the Rioni's right bank, where Aleksandrouli and Mujuretuli become Georgia's best-known semi-sweet red.
A three-step cascade, roughly a hundred metres tall, spilling off the Askhi limestone into the Okatse gorge above Gordi.
A UNESCO-listed Colchic rainforest above Kobuleti, with a ruined bishop's cathedral, a legendary ‘Tamar bridge’ and a lake near 2,000 metres.
A red-brick Golden Age church in the forest near Kareli, where an angel in lapis-lazuli blue points to Christ's empty tomb.
A medieval village-fortress of up to thirty tower-houses in Pirikita Khevsureti; Khevsurs ambushed Russian troops nearby in 1813. One resident remained in 2014.
The Baghuashi eyrie on the Trialeti ridge: a 'rock gate' whose lords held the roads for two centuries and fought kings for the kingdom.
A near-empty highland village on the Georgian Military Road below the Jvari Pass, where the Truso valley opens and a gondola climbs to Gudauri.
A long, unhurried beach town north of Batumi, with a rain-fed Ramsar peat bog behind it where sundew traps insects on the moss.
The ruined walls of Agarani on Azeula crag above Kojori: a royal summer seat, where the chronicles say Queen Tamar died, and a battlefield of 1921.

places.n: Kolkheti National Park and Lake Paliastomi
places.short: Peat bogs, flooded alder forest and the shallow lagoon of Paliastomi, explored by boat from Poti: the wet green heart of ancient Colchis.
Shallow tarns at 2,740 m on the ridge above Mestia, where Ushba's twin horns fill the sky — reached by 4x4, on horseback or by a long climb.
Five hall churches from the 8th to the 16th century, packed inside one wall on a mountain in the Dzama gorge, with 13th-century frescoes.
A 16th-century stronghold of the Mukhrani princes on Mount Sarkineti, half-ruined but still keeping watch where the Ksani meets the Mtkvari.

places.n: The Kukushka narrow-gauge railway and the Tsagveri bridge
places.short: A 37-kilometre, 900-mm line of 1902 climbing from Borjomi to Bakuriani over a lattice bridge that tradition credits to Gustave Eiffel.
A shallow steppe reservoir south of Tbilisi, once a bitter salt pool, where migrating waterbirds rest among the reeds on a great flyway.
A domeless cathedral of 964 on the Javakheti plateau, signed by its architect Sakotsari and carved with a queen, lions, eagles and angels.
A terraced garden near Bagrati where East Asian species outnumber Caucasian ones almost nine to one, and a tiny chapel hides inside a 400-year-old oak.
Kutaisi's two-storey central market: young Imeretian cheese, blue fenugreek by the scoop and churchkhela hanging in rows like strings of amber beads.
Colchian bronzes, a 2,500-year-old silver coin, church silver of western Georgia and eight manuscripts of Rustaveli, on Pushkin Street.
Three synagogues on one Kutaisi street, left by a community that made up a tenth of the city in 1897.
Semi-sweet Saperavi under the Caucasus, a 17th-century river-stone fortress and the house where Ilia Chavchavadze was born.
A small reservoir behind an earth dam at the foot of the Caucasus, with rowing boats, a lakeside resort and the forested slopes mirrored in the water.
Batumi's southernmost beach: a kilometre of pebbles and clear water where the mountains crowd down to the sea.
A Golden Age domed church in white dressed stone at the dead end of a wooded Trialeti gorge, once a scriptorium, part of whose treasury is now in Moscow.
A crag-top fortress above the Mashavera near Bolnisi, entered through a tunnel in the rock and held by the Toreli, the Baratashvili and Daud Khan.
A small 10th-century church roofed in azure tile, inside the forest citadel on the Akhmeta–Tianeti road that a king once failed to take.
A quiet resort village above the Borjomi road, with a legendary battle of 1609 and the house-museum of Dimitri Kipiani, once a refuge for Georgia's writers.
Kutaisi's drama company, rooted in the Georgian-language stage of 1861, plays to an 830-seat hall in a rotund house behind the Colchis Fountain.
Georgia's oldest nature reserve, founded in 1912: beech forest, waterfalls and a two-to-three-day trek to a glacial lake on the Dagestan ridge.
A Lechkhumi hill village where Georgians, Jews, Greeks and Armenians once traded in one square, and where a 10th-century Hebrew Torah codex was found.
A shallow volcanic lake on the Javakheti plateau, nowhere deeper than 85 cm and protected as a Ramsar wetland for the birds that rest on its shores.
A shallow plateau lake drained completely in 1968–1980, refilled in 1997, and now a migration stop for cranes, storks and pelicans.
A 9 km² lake at 2,108 m on the Javakheti plateau and a Ramsar wetland since 2020: one of Georgia's key waterbird sites, rare pelicans included.
Guria's northern gateway: birthplace of Noe Zhordania, a hotbed of the 1905 peasant revolt, and the last big stop before the sea.
A hilltop church in Svaneti's Latali community, painted in 1140 by Mikael Maghlakeli, with a Georgian king's coronation on its wall.
A five-storey Khevsur tower-house of the 16th–17th centuries, standing guard over the road to Shatili beyond the Datvisjvari Pass.
A waterfall in the heart of Old Tbilisi: five minutes from the sulphur baths, a sandstone gorge with old balconies hanging over its edge.
The quiet centre of Lower Svaneti in the Tskhenistskali valley: Svan towers, beech forest, and a town fountain that never got its goddess.
The Romanovs' red-brick summer palace on the Mtkvari just outside Borjomi, lit in 1898 by what is called the first hydroelectric plant in the Russian Empire.
A carved stone hall church on a village hilltop south of Ozurgeti, with a bell tower dated 1422 and a three-towered fortress two kilometres away.
A brackish lake on the plateau behind Saburtalo, ringed by a running path: the Caucasus on the horizon, the capital at your back.
A 9th–10th-century shrine of St George on a 2,200 m ridge above Mleta, where highlanders swore their gravest oaths and still bring sheep on Lomisoba.
A once-forgotten lake at the foot of the Caucasus, turned into a resort in 2008, above a wine village with more history than it lets on.
A Colchic forest valley on the Turkish border, where gunsmiths once forged flintlocks prized as far away as Istanbul.
A 50-metre waterfall and a parapet-less stone arch over the Adjaristsqali, less than half a kilometre apart, under an hour inland from Batumi.
A ruined royal stronghold on the summit above the wine village of Manavi, with three small churches inside a citadel where a Kakhetian king kept court.
An early-medieval cathedral among pines at 1,200 m, founded by tradition in the 4th century and rebuilt in the 11th, in an old garrison resort.
An Art Nouveau people's house on Marjanishvili Street, home since 1930 to the company Kote Marjanishvili founded — Tbilisi's 'social theatre'.
A market town on the Algeti where Georgian and Azerbaijani share the street, tea comes by the pot, and in 1625 Saakadze fought the Safavids at nearby Marabda.
The Abasha river's deep green water between limestone walls up to 70 m high: a 700 m walkway, a short boat ride and the Dadianis' bathing place.
On the hill where Mingrelians once worshipped an oak, the cathedral of Chkondidi, carved with Daniel and his lions, looks out over Imereti and Samegrelo.
A Tsitsishvili castle-palace in the Dzama valley that King Rostom of Kartli failed to take in 1640, with a seven-storey tower and an arched belfry.
Upper Svaneti's capital at 1,500 m: medieval towers in family yards, the 897 Adishi Gospels in the museum, and trails leading off in every direction.
A thirteenth-century church on a cliff over the Mtkvari that survived a citadel, a prison, Beria and a theatre — with old Tbilisi spread out below.
A 13th-century monastery set beneath a limestone overhang above the Kvirila gorge, reached from Chiatura by a long stair and an arched tunnel.
A horseshoe bend of the Alazani deep in Vashlovani, where the river is the border with Azerbaijan: cliffs, fast dark water and a border post.
A ruined Racha stronghold on a crag near Tsesi, granted by a king of Imereti in the 1530s and still one of the hardest castles in Georgia to reach.
A fall of some twenty metres in Colchic forest, and a single-arched medieval bridge nearby — a cool hour's escape from Batumi.
An 18th-century Tsereteli stronghold strung along a limestone crest above Sachkhere, named for a dare: “come and see”.
A cliff-top monastery in a bend of the Tskaltsitela gorge, where pilgrims stoop beneath the relics of two 8th-century martyrs.
A 5,054 m sleeping volcano above Stepantsminda: Amirani's prison in myth, a hermits' cave at 4,000 m, and glaciers that still reshape the valley below.
A 2,002-metre limestone massif in Lechkhumi: a summit that looks sliced off with a knife, a cave of royal treasure and a Prometheus legend.
The twin-summited, 4,710 m 'Matterhorn of the Caucasus' above Svaneti, home, the Svans said, of Dali, goddess of the hunt.
An 11th-century church at 1,840 m on the Racha range, with carved warrior saints, an Ottoman legend and a sultan's helmet among its old treasures.
Moss-grown terraces round St David's church, halfway up the holy mountain: Griboyedov and Nino, Ilia, Vazha, Galaktion and Georgia's quarrels.
Tbilisi's highest balcony: a 1905 funicular lifts you to a Ferris wheel on the lip of the ridge, with the whole city turning below.
UNESCO-listed Colchic rainforest on the ridge behind Batumi: a 28-metre waterfall, moss on every stone, and some of the heaviest rain in Georgia.
A slender two-tier waterfall on a pale limestone cliff above the mining town of Tkibuli, in the Okriba hills at almost 1,000 metres.
Lechkhumi's cliff-top stronghold above Tsageri, with towers named like battle cries and, by tradition, the grave of Maximus the Confessor.
A medieval fortress-village of dry-laid schist on a crag above the Ardoti valley, 11 km beyond Shatili — saved from ruin and honoured by Europa Nostra.
The Gurian valley village behind Georgia's market-leading mineral water: a spring found in 1905, tradition says, by buffalo who knew better.
Hairpins up a 300-metre limestone wall, and at the top Racha opens flat and green, with the Shaori lake and an empty Soviet resort town.
A hilltop St George in Upper Svaneti: inside, Tevdore's frescoes of 1130; outside, an east wall of arches, painted saints and carved animals.
A wine village on the Lopota under the Caucasus, with its own appellation, an 18th-century fortified enclosure and a winery founded in 1883.
Sixteen centuries of wall on the Sololaki ridge above the Old Town: Tbilisi's citadel, its oldest silhouette and its widest view.
Fifty-four Pirosmanis in four rooms on Rustaveli Avenue, in a gallery co-founded by a painter who died for defying Beria.
A 250-metre karst cave near Terjola, four halls over two floors, ending in a seven-metre-thick column of stone that seals the way on.
A 6th-century monastery on a wooded spur above the Alazani valley, with a bishop's palace, a royal fresco and a cellar of buried qvevri.
A cream villa in the Imeretian lowland where a Zurich-trained reformer built Georgia's only wind engine and ordered a sundial from Paris.
Bagrat III's cathedral of 1010–1014 in Racha, its facades carved with the Transfiguration, the Second Coming and a bestiary of real and fabulous beasts.
Eight kilometres of beech forest and stream crossings in Georgia's oldest reserve, ending at a stepped waterfall with a cold pool.
A 6th-century cathedral older than Jvari, felled by earthquakes, now kept by nuns inside a fortified wall on the western edge of Sagarejo.
A memorial museum in Zenobani, the Gurian hill village where Nodar Dumbadze grew up with his grandparents after the 1937 purges took his parents.
The walled capital of ancient Egrisi above the Tekhuri gorge, fought over by Byzantium and Persia in the 6th century and still being excavated.
A 15th–16th-century Armenian church a stone's throw from Sioni, locked since 1995 — its story now told by its walls, gate and courtyard gravestones.
A tiny warm-sulphur resort deep in the forests of Borjomi-Kharagauli, where the water has been treating skin complaints since 1856.
A three-step cascade of 100–120 metres at the head of the Ochkhomuri river, half an hour's walk from Kurzu in the hills north of Martvili.
A 780-metre walkway pinned to a limestone wall above the Okatse river, reached on foot through the old Dadiani forest at Gordi.

places.n: Okros Chardakhi (Palace of the Imeretian Kings)
places.short: The last surviving hall of the Imeretian kings' Kutaisi residence: a two-storey house above the Rioni, shaded by a plane tree some 800 years old.
The Jaqelis' 'golden fortress': ten-metre walls grown into a crag above the Kvabliani valley, where a princess held out in the Ottoman war of 1578.
The slate towers of Keselo over Omalo, shepherd villages north of the Caucasus watershed and a gravel pass open only in summer.
Georgia's third-largest synagogue (1895): a Moorish Revival hall of honey-coloured stone under a ribbed dome, built for a community now counted in families.
Racha's old ducal seat on the Rioni: a honey-stone synagogue, a museum of 14,000 objects and the last cash machine before the high valleys.
A 67-metre waterfall fed by the underground river of the Toba First Cave, in the karst forest above Martvili: seldom visited and hard to reach.
A village assembled on a wooded hill above Vake, where a Khevsur tower, an early basilica from Tianeti and a Megrelian maize granary stand as neighbours.
Tbilisi's old market square, restored in 2019: flower stalls, a small fountain garden and the doorway into the lanes of Sololaki.
A little-known canyon near Moedani in Guria that splits into two “doors”: an easy walk to a waterfall on the left, a climbers' route on the right.

places.n: Ozurgeti Drama Theatre (Alexandre Tsutsunava State Drama Theatre)
places.short: A white neoclassical giant in the town garden — begun in 1934, finished in 1962, restored in 2020 — with a 750-seat hall and a revolving stage.
Guria's capital since the days of the Gurieli princes: a green town on three terraces, with a drama theatre that has played since 1868.
The upper Alazani valley north of Akhmeta, home for nearly two centuries to the Chechen-speaking Kists: brick mosques, wooded slopes, open doors.
Georgia's largest lake, never deeper than 3.3 metres, and deep, steep-sided Tabatskuri, both lying at 2,000 metres on the treeless volcanic Javakheti plateau.
A deserted tower-village on the left bank of the Pirikiti Alazani, where a seven-storey tower-house still keeps watch over the track to Girevi.
The old heart of Mtiuleti, where the White and Black Aragvi meet in two colours and khinkali are treated as a matter of local honour.
Justinian's 6th-century fortress-city on two rocky hills above the sea at Tsikhisdziri, fought over through the whole of the Lazic War.
A Colchian settlement and Greek-Colchian necropolis where the Choloki meets the sea: open ground today, its finds kept in Batumi's museum.
Pirosmani's 1898 village house, now a museum holding 14 of his paintings and a lithograph of Picasso's portrait of him.
A carved 13th-century church of the Virgin in a deep, wooded fold of the Khrami valley, ringed by two walls and reached by a rough forest road.
An 11th-century church and a living convent on the southern shore of Lake Paravani, at 2,073 m, where tradition says St Nino paused.
A cast-iron tower made in London in 1862 and lit in 1864 at the mouth of the Rioni — 160 iron steps, a small museum, and a light that still works.
Georgia's working port at the mouth of the Rioni: a radial town built around a concrete echo of Hagia Sophia, with an English cast-iron lighthouse.
Six lit halls in the Imereti karst, found in 1984, guarded through the lean years by one villager, and, for a few lari more, left by boat on a hidden lake.
Eleven white 'petals' on steel trees beside the Mtkvari: the Fuksas building where renewing a passport comes with a piece of architecture.

places.fee: lower town free; citadel ticket (check locally)
places.short: Akhaltsikhe's walled hill, where a Jaqeli palace, an 18th-century mosque and an Orthodox church share one enclosure above the old town.
King Rostom's 17th-century brick bridge over the Khrami, 175 metres long, stranded in the neutral strip between Georgia and Azerbaijan.
A 996-metre saddle of the Likhi Range where Georgia's waters divide between Black Sea and Caspian, with a 1982 tunnel below and an old forest road above.
A 7th-century monastery deep in the forested Tedzami gorge, reached by fords and gravel, with a medieval stone bridge that still carries walkers.
A stone village of Khevsureti at 2,000 m under the teeth of Chaukhi, with house-sized glacial boulders above it and the Abudelauri lakes beyond.
It crowned a boy-king, hosted David the Builder's council, fell to Timur and rose again: Ruisi's patched, polychrome walls keep every entry.
Levan II Dadiani's frontier stronghold above the Enguri: an ivy-bound citadel that housed Ottoman garrisons and saw the victory of 1779.
A kilometre and a half of opera, parliament, frescoed church and plane-tree shade: Tbilisi's showcase and the stage of its political memory.
Georgia's largest theatre, a Rococo wedding cake on Rustaveli Avenue — stage of Akhmeteli and Sturua, with a basement painted by Gudiashvili and Kakabadze.
A city built twice on the Mtkvari: an ancient royal fortress-town, then Stalin's steel city, with a Soviet race circuit and a vast car market.
Georgia's oldest national park, an hour from Tbilisi: a road-tunnel of beech and oak, white in January, copper in October, beside a ruined Soviet pioneer camp.
A small Kvirila-valley town with a Tsereteli castle, a 1907 stone railway station, an idle Soviet cable car and bold industrial mosaics.
The country house of Georgia's "Father of the Nation": manuscripts, paintings and his belongings, a few kilometres from where he was killed in 1907.
Limestone pillars rising from Lechkhumi's forest above the Rioni gorge: a three-kilometre trail, a medieval church ruin and, very likely, no one else.
A spa town in a fir-dark gorge of the Meskheti Range, named after the deer that led hunters to its salty, rust-stained springs.
Rain-carved volcanic cliffs above the Terek near Sioni. The name means 'refuge': villagers once climbed into these rocks to hide from raiders.
The Dadiani 'house of feasting' north of Martvili: a stone palace with a qvevri set into its great hall, near the old home of the Ojaleshi grape.
A convent on Nigoiti hill whose site, tradition says, was chosen by three doves, and where, the nuns say, the liturgy never stopped, even under Soviet rule.
A ruined city 2.5 km long on a triangular promontory where the Khrami and Chivchavi gorges meet: ancient Kartli's stronghold, sacked in 1440.
A cathedral of 1030 near Igoeti; its carved east front, a great cross over two stone diamonds, was copied by Georgian masons for generations.
Where Nino lived among the brambles and Georgia's first Christian king lies buried: a working convent five minutes up the street from Svetitskhoveli.
A 7th-century free-cross church barely eleven metres tall that still commands the plain where the Dzama meets the Mtkvari.
The Jaqeli family's monastery at the head of a wooded valley above Akhaltsikhe, its walls painted with 14th-century portraits of Samtskhe's rulers.
Walls of huge unmortared boulders on the edge of the Javakheti plateau above Khertvisi: a stronghold perhaps three thousand years old.
Georgia's last village on the Black Sea: a Laz settlement cut in two in 1921, deep clear water, and a sunset straight into open sea.
Some 200 dinosaur footprints in the rock, a dripping karst cave and a glass deck over Colchic forest, about ten kilometres from Kutaisi.
A karst cave beside Prometheus Cave where a 13,300-year-old bone yielded the genome that defined the Caucasus Hunter-Gatherers.
Racha's largest lake is man-made: a 1950s reservoir in a karst basin below the Nakerala cliffs, with an emptied Soviet town on its western shore.
More than sixty flat-roofed towers fused into one wall in the Argun gorge near the Chechen border — Khevsureti's fortress-village, reachable only in summer.
A monastery of St George on a forested mountain above Teleti, named after a legendary black-cloaked rider — with its own icon school and wine.
A glacier-fed double waterfall below Ushba, reached by a forest trail from Mazeri: loudest in June and wrapped in its own cold spray.

places.n: Shekvetili and the Black Sea Arena
places.short: A pine-shaded beach village between Ureki and Kobuleti, home of the Black Sea Arena: 9,000 seats under a roof that opens to the sky.
Sixty hectares of relocated giants by the sea: old trees brought here by road and barge, with flamingos standing in the lake between them.
Two joined churches above the Bzhuzhi river: a Gurieli burial place, a bishop's seat, and a castle that Russian troops razed in 1820.
Two stone villages at the eastern edge of Tusheti: a whitewashed 19th-century church and a ruined fortress a few kilometres from Dagestan.
A 6th-century monastery deep in a pale limestone gorge west of Mtskheta, grown around the cave where the hermit Shio chose to live, die and be buried.
An eight-kilometre walk from Ushguli to the source of the Enguri, under the ice wall of Shkhara, at 5,203 m the highest mountain in Georgia.
Strabo’s Sarapana: a hilltop fort over the Dzirula–Kvirila confluence, where the river road ended and the land road began.
A Soviet-era mountain spa at 1,520 metres beneath the main Caucasus ridge — conifer forest, carbonated springs, and the memory of August 2023.
Every Orthodox Easter the two halves of a Gurian village fight over a 16-kilo leather ball, and the winning ball ends up on a grave.
King Erekle's walled refuge on a ridge at 790 metres: towers, cobbled lanes and the whole Alazani Valley laid out below the Caucasus.
A honey-coloured cathedral in the old town, destroyed and rebuilt for fourteen centuries, where St Nino's grapevine cross rests in candlelight.
A 13th-century hall church in a forested valley of Upper Adjara: abandoned under the Ottomans, sketched by a scout in 1874, alive again since 1990.
A 14th-century Amilakhvari stronghold on a high ridge above the Lekhura valley, whose only gate was set two metres off the ground.
The stone manor at Skhvitori, 3 km from Sachkhere, where the poet Akaki Tsereteli was born in 1840 and died in 1915.
A wooded gorge near Tsalenjikha where cattle found the healing spring first — today the spa is gone, leaving quiet woods and scattered ancient ruins.
A former seat of Khevi's governors at 1,760 m: a stone tower on a walled crag and giant faces carved into boulders by the sculptor Merab Piranishvili.

places.n: Sololaki and its Art Nouveau Entrances
places.short: A merchants' quarter under the Sololaki ridge where the real show is indoors: painted stairwells, coloured glass and the Writers' House on Machabeli Street.
A high town on the Terek, birthplace of the writer Alexander Kazbegi, where Kazbek's white cone rises over the rooftops and every road into Khevi begins.
A citadel on a rock at the old fork of the roads west over the Likhi range and south to Borjomi, home to one of Georgia's best-known legends.

places.n: Svaneti Museum of History and Ethnography
places.short: Svaneti's strongroom: beaten-silver icons, Gospel books and the Adishi Gospels of 897, gathered by a founder who was shot a year later.
Georgia's mother church: an 11th-century cathedral said to guard Christ's robe, with kings beneath its floor and its architect's carved hand on the wall.
A pine-wooded village some 1,000 m up on Tbilisi's southern rim, with a name meaning "dry lake" and a hard-fought February in 1921.
A monastery rebuilt in 1995–2001 on the ridge facing Narikala — a hill shahs and kings fought over, with Old Tbilisi laid out below.
A low hillock south of the Dali Mta reservoir where grey mud, gas and a sheen of oil seep up without pause: Vashlovani's strangest corner.
A gorge garden behind the walls of Narikala, where the city falls silent within minutes and one path follows a stream to a waterfall.
A 1939 Stalin-era rotunda on the hill above Heroes' Square: Tbilisi's 2,000-seat circus, left to decay in the 1990s and back in business since 2011.
Georgia's largest synagogue: red brick, Moorish-tinged arches and a painted prayer hall, built in 1904–1911 by Jews from Akhaltsikhe.
An 1818 merchants' caravanserai on 17th-century vaults beside Sioni Cathedral, now Tbilisi's city-history museum with some 50,000 objects.
The Paliashvili opera house on Rustaveli Avenue: a neo-Moorish façade, a European hall, 175 seasons and the State Ballet of Georgia.
A 1953 reservoir that drowned three salt lakes on the Iori Plateau: Tbilisi's summer beach, a working water supply and shores settled 3,000 years ago.
Founded in 1887: thousands of cocoon varieties in their original 1890s cases, inside a red-brick hall carved with silkworms and moths.
Georgia's oldest zoo, opened in 1927 in the green fold of the Vere valley: an easy family morning with a hard and honest history.
Kakheti's capital on its terrace above the Alazani: Erekle II's palace-fortress, a 900-year-old plane tree, and the Caucasus across the valley.
A broken 6th-century wall on a steep hill above the Rioni plain — the Telephis where Byzantium and Persia fought for western Georgia.

places.n: Telovani Church of the Holy Cross
places.short: An 8th–9th-century triconch on a slope above the Ksani valley, keeping one of Georgia's earliest painted images of the Mandylion, Christ's Holy Face.
A cool upland basin on the upper Iori where Kakhetian rulers once held court, with a reservoir over drowned villages and Bochorma fortress downriver.
A rose-brick church of Queen Tamar's age in the Gujareti valley near Tsagveri, painted inside in 1205–1215 by some of Georgia's finest masters.
A dammed-up karst basin at the foot of the Nakerala cliff: grey-green water, wooded islands and a coal town's quiet back garden.
A cliff town-fortress strung across three rocky hills above the Mtkvari, thrown down by earthquakes and still reached only on foot.

places.n: Toba Waterfall and Arsen Okrojanashvili Cave
places.short: Toba, at 234 metres Georgia's highest cascade, pours from a three-level cave; a marked 5.6 km trail leads to it from First Balda.
The Silver Lake of Mingrelian legend: a 35-metre-deep cirque tarn at 2,650 m on the Egrisi range, three to five days' trek from the road.
A stone church with a square bell tower, built by German colonists on the Trialeti plateau: a Soviet warehouse and cinema, now re-roofed and listed.
About a hundred deer, horses, goats, fish and tiny archers cut into basalt near Gantiadi: Georgia's only prehistoric rock art of its kind.
The treeless cradle of the Terek: fizzing mineral springs, rust-streaked travertine and the empty tower villages of a once-mixed Georgian and Ossetian valley.
Lechkhumi's quiet capital on the Tskhenistskali: a bishop's town, a saint's grave beneath Muri fortress, and Usakhelouri, the wine called 'nameless'.
One of Georgia's oldest bishoprics, south-west of Zugdidi: a domed church of around 1300, rebuilt after the 1614 earthquake, with 17th-century murals.
A Mingrelian cathedral painted in the late 14th century by the Constantinople master Manuel Eugenikos: late Byzantine art of the first rank.
Georgia's largest reservoir by surface: 33.7 km² of cold, wind-whipped water at 1,506 m on the Tsalka plateau, where Bronze Age gold came out of the ground.
A 4th-century foundation remade in dressed sandstone and ringed by an 18th-century fortress wall, in a quiet village just north of Mtskheta.
Alexander Chavchavadze's palace, an English-style park and the cellar where Georgian wine was first bottled the European way, 8 km from Telavi.
An evening funfair in the Shekvetili pines: a white Ferris wheel with red cabins, rides for small children and lights that come on at dusk.
A Soviet spa town laid out in a ring around warm radon springs, where working bathhouses stand beside sanatoriums slowly turning into forest.
A shrine of St George and nine crosses on a cliff-edge summit above the Nakerala Pass, looking over western Georgia towards the sea.
An unpaved pass high on the Trialeti range above Bakuriani, where spruce gives way to subalpine meadow and the road drops towards Lake Tabatskuri.
Built in 626–634 for Prince Stepanoz II, Tsromi was the first Georgian church to raise its dome on four free-standing piers.
A small, soaring domed church of 1212–1222 near Bolnisi, built of golden, wine-red and blue stone and carved from drum to doorway.
The site of Javakheti's oldest centre by the Mtkvari near Vardzia: a 12th–13th-century church on a rock, a carved porch and terraces nobody has dug.
A thirteen-storey karst cave in the Chishura gorge, where Neanderthals camped and someone once laid out cave-bear skulls with care.
A landslide pond on a pine ridge above Vake, six minutes up by gondola: the place Tbilisi goes when the streets below start to bake.
A 9th-century monastery in the Dzirula valley, with 14th-century frescoes and a tower-house of 1141 built by the kingdom's grand chancellor.
A half-cave monastery of St John the Baptist on the wooded slope of Mount Amaghleba, once Guria's school and library; not the Udabno of David Gareja.
Hills striped rust, ochre and pale green around the Mravaltskaro reservoir, on the empty steppe between Udabno and David Gareja.
A lake called 'bottomless' at 2,800 metres above Shovi and Glola, and a glacier scientists watched from 1965 — two days on foot, no shortcuts.
The ridge-top fortress-town above the Iori where, the chronicle says, Vakhtang Gorgasali died of his wounds — 45 km from Tbilisi on the Gombori road.
A secret press of 1903–1906 beneath an Avlabari house, reached down a water well and along a tunnel: Tbilisi's strangest museum.
A town cut into a sandstone ridge above the Mtkvari: rock halls, a stone main street, wine presses and a tunnel to the river, lived in for three millennia.
A long, low basilica of c. 500–600 in what was once ancient Iberia's second city, where David the Builder's church council met in 1103.
Black, magnetite-rich sand, a belt of pines and a sea that stays shallow far from shore: Ureki is Georgia's classic family beach on the Guria coast.
Five tower villages at the head of the Enguri, 2,100 m up under Shkhara — one of Europe's highest year-round communities, and still a working one.
A spa village on both banks of the Rioni, 10 km above Oni, where sparkling, iron-tinged water runs free from pipes among the firs.
A 10th-century church remade as a basilica in the 16th, its walls carrying Georgian inscriptions in two scripts — the quiet core of a border town.
A Colchian city-sanctuary burned in the 1st century BC: hilltop walls and altars above a museum of gold diadems, Greek pottery and bronze.
An 8th-century cave monastery two kilometres from Vardzia, where women in the 15th century inked verses of Rustaveli on a chapel wall.
Queen Tamar's cave monastery above the Mtkvari: some 500 m of cliff in up to nineteen tiers, and a church where Tamar was painted in her lifetime.
Ruined walls on the Rioni where Byzantines fought Persians over 'the city of the rose' and Imereti's last king made his stand against Russia in 1810.
Georgia's dry south-eastern edge: clay badlands, open pistachio woodland and the Alazani on the Azerbaijani border, reached only by 4x4.
The two-room house in a Pshavi village where Luka Razikashvili became Vazha-Pshavela: his rifle, his sister’s saddlebag, and his mountains outside.
A mossy rock on the edge of Ambrolauri where water drips across a heart-shaped cave mouth. The heart was cut by hand, and the story is true.
A summer-only mountain track from Lentekhi to Ushguli, past a dead arsenic works and over a 2,600-metre saddle, with no fuel and no signal.
A small domeless church of 1519 on a hazel-wooded hill south of Samtredia, where on clear days the view reaches Lake Paliastomi and Poti.
A 14th-century monastery in the forested Kvabliani valley west of Akhaltsikhe, with portraits of the Jaqeli princes and one of Georgia's largest bell towers.
On the forested Saguramo ridge above Mtskheta, the hill where John, leader of the Thirteen Assyrian Fathers, settled on the site of a pagan idol.
A 2,182 m summer-only pass over the Meskheti Range, where a rough jeep track climbs out of Colchic forest into flowering meadows above Abastumani.
The Tush people's winter village on the Alazani plain — sheep, wool, an 8th–9th-century basilica — where the road to Tusheti begins.

places.n: Zemo Nikozi Cathedral of the Deity (Ghvtaeba)
places.short: A bishop's cathedral at the edge of occupied Tskhinvali region, founded by tradition on a martyr's grave and burned by air attacks in August 2008.
A Kvirila river town of manganese furnaces and Tsolikouri vines — the natural pause on the E60, with a loud market and Shorapani fortress next door.
Tbilisi's drinking water in a long turquoise lake, laid over a drowned medieval town, with the Military Highway running along its shore.
A Gurian mountain village of Adjarian settlers on the Bakhmaro road, with a painted wooden mosque of 1904 that few drivers ever step into.
The Dadiani princes' garden of 1840 behind their Zugdidi palace: plane avenues, magnolias, cedars and an island lake laid out by a gardener from Trieste.

Gori and Uplistsikhe in One Day
Kvemo Kartli Monasteries in One Day
Racha in Two Days — Churches, Lake and Mountain Villages
Vardzia and Borjomi — the Southern Route
